summary: A UC San Diego Today article, published August 15, 2023 by Christine Clark, reports on a working paper from the Rady School of Management arguing that reducing U.S. inflation from about 3% to the Federal Reserve's 2% target may be hard without raising unemployment and risking a recession. The authors, led by Allan Timmermann, find a steep trade-off between unemployment and inflation when labor markets run hot, as they do now, while the traditional Phillips Curve has flattened over time. Timmermann sees no immediate recession but says one could occur within a year if the Fed holds to its 2% goal.
one_line: A UC San Diego study warns that cutting U.S. inflation to the Fed's 2% target with hot labor markets risks raising unemployment and triggering a recession.
key_facts: The article was published August 15, 2023 and written by Christine Clark of UC San Diego.
U.S. inflation has come down significantly from nearly 9% to 3% while unemployment stays low, according to the article.
The working paper is from the Rady School of Management at the University of California San Diego.
The paper is titled "Breaks in the Phillips Curve: Evidence from Panel Data."
According to the authors, the labor market is behind about half of the rise in inflation, and special pandemic-related supply factors explain the other half.
Allan Timmermann is a distinguished professor of finance at the Rady School of Management and co-author of the working paper.
Timmermann said "there is a steep trade-off between unemployment and inflation when the economy is running hot as it is now."
The Phillips Curve has flattened significantly over time due to events such as China's integration into the world trade system in 2000.
Co-authors are Jonathan H. Wright of Johns Hopkins University and Simon Smith of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.
The researchers used data on U.S. metropolitan areas, states, industries and 28 European Union countries, analyzed with a panel regression.
Wages continue to rise at close to 5%, which makes it very hard to bring overall inflation to 2%, according to Timmermann.
Timmermann sees no immediate signs of a recession, but one could occur in the next year or so if the Fed sticks to its 2% inflation commitment.
If interest rates stay higher for longer, mortgage rates would rise, house prices would fall, and firms issuing bonds would face higher interest payments.
